content: Copper-containing intrauterine devices (IUDs) and depot progestogens are both highly effective, long-acting, reversible contraceptive methods, but they differ in their risk and benefit profiles. The purpose of this study was to compare the contraceptive efficacy and non-contraceptive effects of copper IUDs versus depot progestogens. A comprehensive search was conducted in June 2009 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, PubMed, Popline, ClinicalTrials.gov, the Current Controlled Trials metaRegister, EMBASE, and LILACS. Study authors were also contacted to identify relevant randomized trials. The review included randomized trials that directly compared women using copper-containing IUDs with those using depot progestogens. Two studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. In one study involving HIV-infected women, participants were given the choice between a copper IUD, depot progestogens, or oral contraceptives. Most women in this study opted for depot progestogens, and the study was included in the review under a mixed hormonal contraception subgroup. The findings demonstrated that copper IUDs were significantly more effective at preventing pregnancy compared to depot progestogens or hormonal contraception. The risk ratio (RR) for pregnancy prevention with copper IUDs was 0.47 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.26 to 0.85), indicating a lower likelihood of pregnancy in the IUD group. Additionally, HIV disease progression was less frequent in women using copper IUDs compared to those using depot progestogens or hormonal contraception, with a risk ratio of 0.66 (95% CI: 0.46 to 0.96). There was no statistically significant difference in the rates of pelvic inflammatory disease between the two groups. However, discontinuation rates varied between the studies. In one study, women using copper IUDs were less likely to discontinue their assigned method, while in the other study, women using hormonal contraception (with the option to switch between various hormonal methods) had lower discontinuation rates. The authors concluded that, in the populations studied, copper IUDs were more effective than hormonal contraception in preventing pregnancy. However, there is an urgent need for high-quality research to further investigate the potential effects of these contraceptive methods on HIV acquisition, seroconversion, and the progression of HIV/AIDS.
